question: In its judgment in the cases WM and Sovim v Luxembourg Business Registers (C-37/20 and C-601/20), the Court of Justice of the European Union ruled that open public access to information on ultimate beneficial owners (UBOs) constitutes a serious breach of the rights to respect for private and family life and to protection of personal data, as protected by Articles 7 and 8 of the Charter.

Directive (EU) 2024/1640 reintroduces access for persons with a ‘legitimate interest’. For certain categories, including journalists and civil-society organisations, such an interest is assumed to apply and a link to the legal entity concerned does not have to be demonstrated.
The Directive also stipulates that UBOs will not be informed about which journalist or civilsociety organisation has consulted their personal data. 1.

How is the Commission guaranteeing that access based on an assumed ‘legitimate interest’, for which no concrete link to the entity concerned has to be demonstrated, complies with the requirements of necessity and proportionality highlighted by the Court in the Sovim judgment?
In the Commission’s view, how is the right of UBOs to the protection of their personal data guaranteed if they cannot find out which journalist or civil-society organisation has consulted their data?
How can a UBO verify retrospectively whether data was actually consulted within the framework of a ‘legitimate interest’?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.11.2026) Article 12 of Directive (EU) 2024/16401 addresses the findings of the Court of Justice in cases C-37/20 and C-601/202 by restricting access to information held in interconnected central registers to persons with a legitimate interest and limiting the information accessible.

Under Article 12(2), journalists and civil-society organisations engaged in anti-money laundering and countering financing of terrorism work are deemed to have legitimate interest. Article 13 of that Directive requires Member States to ensure that entities in charge of central beneficial ownership registers verify the existence of such legitimate interest.
Both provisions aim to keep access to information necessary and proportionate without impeding investigations.

Article 12(4) of the Directive requires central beneficial ownership registers to keep records of persons accessing information held in those registers and allows an ultimate beneficial owner to obtain information on consultations as provided for in Article 15(1)(c) of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of the European Parliament and of the Council on General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)3.

Recital 41 of Directive (EU) 2024/1640 states that, to reconcile data protection with freedom of expression and information for journalists in accordance with Article 85 of the GDPR, and to ensure the role of civil society organisations in prevention, investigation and detection of money laundering, predicate offences or terrorist financing in accordance with Article 23(1) (d), of the GDPR, entities in charge of central registers should not share with beneficial owners information on processing of their data by those categories of the public, but only the fact that persons acting for purposes of journalism or for civil society organisations have consulted their data.
1 Directive (EU) 2024/1640 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 31 May 2024 on the mechanisms

to be put in place by Member States for the prevention of the use of the financial system for the purposes of money laundering or terrorist financing, amending Directive(EU) 2019/1937, and amending and repealing Directive (EU) 2015/849 (OJ L, 2024/1640, 19.6.2024, http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2024/1640/oj).
